content: Hepatitis B is a significant global health issue and ranks among the most prevalent infectious diseases worldwide. Despite a decline in global prevalence due to effective vaccination programs, over 264 million individuals remain chronically infected with the hepatitis B virus (HBV), and approximately one million people die annually from acute or chronic complications of the disease. Chronic HBV carriers face an elevated risk of developing cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). While the majority of carriers do not experience hepatic complications, 15% to 40% will develop severe sequelae over their lifetime. HBV is transmitted through perinatal, percutaneous, and sexual exposure, as well as close person-to-person contact, particularly via open cuts and sores. This is especially common among children in hyperendemic regions. HBV is a circular, partially double-stranded DNA virus with a genome of approximately 3200 nucleotides. Its genome encodes four open reading frames responsible for the production of envelope (PreS1, PreS2, S), core (core, precore), polymerase, and X proteins. HBV is classified into eight genotypes (A through H), which exhibit distinct geographic distributions and may influence disease progression and therapeutic response. Acute hepatitis B is typically a self-limiting condition, with over 95% of patients achieving full recovery. However, in 0.1% to 1% of cases, it may progress to fulminant hepatitis. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic infection to cholestatic hepatitis with jaundice. Symptoms generally appear approximately six weeks post-infection, coinciding with the detection of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) in the serum, elevated levels of immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies to the viral core antigen (IgM anti-HBc), and detectable HBV DNA. Chronic infection is indicated by the persistence of HBsAg in the serum for more than six months, along with elevated liver enzymes and histological evidence of chronic hepatitis. Significant advancements in the treatment of chronic hepatitis B have been made since the 1990s. Interferon (IFN) alfa, an immunomodulatory agent, was the primary treatment option after its approval in the early 1990s. The therapeutic goals for HBV infection include reducing viral load and improving hepatic function. IFN therapy has been associated with HBsAg clearance, while nucleotide/nucleoside analogues can effectively control viraemia and are often considered lifelong treatments. The introduction of nucleoside analogues and pegylated interferon (peg-IFN) has expanded treatment options, leading to the development of multiple international practice guidelines. These guidelines recommend both nucleoside analogues and peg-IFN as first-line treatments, though the optimal choice for individual patients remains debated. Currently, seven medications are approved for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B: IFN-α, peg-IFN, lamivudine, adefovir, entecavir, telbivudine, and tenofovir. IFN-α therapy has been shown to increase HBsAg loss by 6% compared to natural seroconversion rates, but its high cost and significant adverse effects often lead to treatment discontinuation. Lamivudine is a cost-effective option but is associated with a high risk of viral resistance. Newer antiviral agents, such as entecavir, tenofovir, and tenofovir alafenamide, are potent HBV inhibitors with high barriers to resistance, making them preferred choices for treatment. Adefovir offers advantages similar to lamivudine but with a lower risk of resistance, while telbivudine is another potent HBV inhibitor, though it has reported toxicities. Despite these advancements, the cost of nucleotide/nucleoside analogues may limit their accessibility. Entecavir, a cyclopentyl guanosine nucleoside analogue, has demonstrated potent suppression of HBV replication with low rates of genotypic resistance, even with long-term use in treatment-naive patients. It selectively inhibits HBV DNA polymerase and disrupts viral replication at three critical stages: polymerase priming, reverse transcription of the DNA strand, and DNA-dependent plus-strand DNA synthesis. The recommended dose of entecavir for nucleoside-treatment-naive adults and adolescents aged 16 years or older is 0.5 mg once daily. For patients with a history of HBV viraemia while on lamivudine or with known lamivudine or telbivudine resistance mutations, the dose is increased to 1 mg once daily. Pharmacokinetic studies indicate that entecavir has an intracellular half-life of approximately 15 hours, with peak plasma concentrations reached within 0.5 to 1.5 hours and steady-state levels achieved after 6 to 10 days of daily administration. It is primarily excreted unchanged by the kidneys, necessitating dosage adjustments for patients with creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min, including those on dialysis. However, no dosage adjustment is required for liver disease. Two multinational phase III trials have compared entecavir with lamivudine in nucleoside-naive patients. In HBeAg-positive patients, 68% to 89% achieved alanine aminotransferase normalization, and 58% to 74% had undetectable HBV DNA after 48 weeks of treatment. HBeAg clearance and seroconversion rates were comparable between the two drugs, though surface antigen loss was rare. Entecavir demonstrated superior antiviral efficacy compared to lamivudine in treatment-naive patients with chronic hepatitis B, with a similar safety and adverse reaction profile. Meta-analyses of antiviral therapy for chronic HBV infection have shown potential benefits, including clearance of serum HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA, normalization of liver enzymes, and reduced long-term complications such as HCC recurrence after curative treatment. However, these studies are limited by high risk of bias and small sample sizes. Current uncertainties regarding the effectiveness of entecavir have prompted a Cochrane Review to evaluate its benefits and harms compared to other antiviral drugs. Additionally, a planned review will compare entecavir with placebo or no intervention in patients with chronic hepatitis B. These findings will be compared with results from a network systematic review assessing the effects of antiviral treatments for chronic hepatitis B.
